w: What's tested Terms: occlusion vs articulation, neutral zone, occlusal plane, curves of Spee and Wilson, compensating curve, sphere of Monson, crossbite MIP vs centric occlusion vs centric relation (the exam uses CO only to mean "teeth touching with the joints seated") Angle classes, cusp-fossa vs cusp-marginal ridge, and "what cusp hits where" with the fence post Working, non-working and protrusive contacts; canine guidance, group function, mutually protected occlusion The five determinants and what makes posterior cusps taller or shorter VDO, VDR, freeway space; the envelope of motion in three planes; postural vs clinical rest position; Bennett movement; articulator parts Dr. Givan opened the course by revisiting last spring's introduction, because "this is fundamental. This is sort of the starting point." The review has three parts: static and dynamic occlusion, mandibular motion, and articulators. He also pointed to a help sheet in Canvas, "Help! What cusp hits where?", because questions on which cusp contacts where come up "repeatedly through the years" on exams and boards. Speaking the same language Occlusion is the static relationship between the incising or masticating surfaces of the maxillary and mandibular teeth (or tooth analogs). Articulation is the static and dynamic contact relationship during function. People use them interchangeably, "but they're not quite the same." The neutral zone is the potential space between the lips and cheeks on one side and the tongue on the other, where their forces are equal. It is thought to guide where teeth develop. Restored or orthodontically moved teeth should be within it: put something in the way of those muscles "and they'll just sort of knock it out of the way." An imbalance shows up developmentally, for example as an anterior open bite. The occlusal plane (older term: plane of occlusion) is the average plane established by the incisal and occlusal surfaces. It is not really flat; it is the planar mean of their curvature, and it is one of the keys to good outcomes when rebuilding a patient. Curve of Spee Sagittal (median) From the mandibular canine cusp tip along the buccal cusp tips of the premolars and molars, through the anterior border of the ramus, to the anterior-most part of the condyle (Graf von Spee, 1890) Curve of Wilson Frontal Mediolateral curve of the cusps in both arches: concave in the mandibular arch, convex in the maxillary. Follows the posterior teeth erupting tipped (maxillary angled out, mandibular angled in) Compensating curve Both The anteroposterior and mediolateral curving of artificial teeth, used to develop balanced (denture) occlusion. "Curve of Spee is specific for teeth" Sphere of Monson Three-dimensional Each cusp conforms to an imaginary sphere of about 4-inch radius centered near the glabella How the arches fit Opposing cusps ideally meet along the central fossa line. Normally the maxillary lingual cusps sit in the mandibular central fossa line and the mandibular buccal cusps sit in the maxillary central fossa line. Reverse articulation (crossbite) flips it: maxillary buccal and mandibular lingual cusps in the opposing fossae. It comes from a discrepancy in arch size or eruption, and "there is absolutely functionally no problem with this." After bone loss most posterior implant crowns have to be built in crossbite; just design them so they don't trap the cheek. The maxillary arch is longer and wider than the mandibular, but not by much (average arch length about 128 vs 126 mm, with great variation). Arch length runs from the distal of the last tooth on one side, through the contact areas, to the distal of the last tooth on the other. Posterior tooth form The occlusal table, between the buccal and lingual cusp tips, is about 50-60% of the tooth's buccolingual width. Each cusp has a mesial and a distal incline. Proximal contacts sit buccal to the central fossa line, so the lingual embrasures are larger, which returns food toward the tongue. The tongue, cheeks (buccinator) and lips keep replacing food on the table; the tongue works as "a knife, fork, and spoon." Which Maxillary lingual, mandibular buccal Maxillary buccal, mandibular lingual Other names Supporting, holding, "stamp" cusps Shearing or guiding cusps Shape Broad, rounded, about 1/3 of the B-L width Sharp with definite tips, about 1/6 of the B-L width Job Maintain the vertical dimension of occlusion; final crushing contact Functional outer aspect shears food (ideally near-contact, no true contact); minimize cheek and tongue impingement; hold the bolus on the table MIP, centric occlusion and centric relation "Terminology is a real problem, especially in occlusion," because our ideas started with dentures. Maximum intercuspation (MIP, MICP, ICP) is the complete intercuspation of the teeth independent of condylar position: a tooth-to-tooth relationship set by muscle engrams to protect the teeth. It is not constant: every restoration, tooth movement or loss changes it, so "I'll just restore to MIP" can get you into trouble. In about 90% of people the joints are not in their stable orthopedic position when the teeth are in MIP. Centric occlusion (CO) is the tooth contact when the mandible is in centric relation. "Centric" means the joint is centered; "when you hear centric, you immediately turn on, oh, we're talking joint." If Dr. Givan could take one term out of the world with a giant eraser, it would be centric occlusion, because so many people use it to mean MIP. On his exams, centric occlusion always means the contact with the joints seated, never MIP. MIP is neuromuscularly determined; CO is structurally determined. About 90% of people have a slide between the CO contact and MIP, averaging 1.25 ± 1 mm; a slide that deviates left or right tends to be more problematic. Only about 10% have CO and MIP coincident, which is also where we deliberately rebuild patients who need full reconstruction. The CO contact is often unstable; when we close into it without neuromuscular protection (our muscles seat the joints all the time, especially asleep), we get wear facets, fractures and mobility, which are very common findings. Centric relation (CR) is the maxillomandibular relationship in which the condyles articulate with the thinnest avascular portion of their discs, the complex in the anterior-superior position against the slopes of the articular eminences. It is independent of tooth contact, clinically discernable when the mandible is directed superiorly and anteriorly (bimanual manipulation, or a leaf gauge or Lucia jig), and restricted to pure rotation about the transverse horizontal axis. His short version: "it's where the condyle is seated in the joint. That's it." Our teeth touch only about 18 minutes a day; the rest of the time the muscles seat the condyles. What it is Teeth maximally intercuspated Teeth touching with the joints seated Joints seated (a joint position) Depends on Teeth; neuromuscular feedback The seated joint Joint anatomy, not teeth Stable over time? No: changes with every change in the occlusion Yes (the joint), but the tooth contact is often unstable Yes: reproducible starting point Key number Differ in about 90% of people; slide 1.25 ± 1 mm Pure rotation up to about 20-25 mm Angle classification Class I (neutroclusion) Normal interdigitation About 70% "Class I malocclusion" = normal molars but crowding or rotations elsewhere Class II (distoclusion) Mandibular first molar distal to the maxillary first molar About 25% Division 1: narrow arch, protruding incisors. Division 2: square arch, retruded centrals, flared laterals, deep overlap (hard to restore) Class III (mesioclusion) Mandibular first molar mesial to the maxillary first molar About 5% Incisors usually edge to edge or in anterior crossbite Class IV (retired) Distal on one side, mesial on the other - Now each side is classified separately You can classify at the canines or the first molars. Exam rule: if a question doesn't name the class, assume Class I (after checking it isn't implied indirectly). Two contact variations: cusp-marginal ridge (the mandibular second premolar buccal cusp and the mandibular molar mesiobuccal cusps land in the opposing embrasures; one tooth against two; most adults; Payne's waxing technique) and cusp-fossa (centric cusps in the opposing fossae; tooth to tooth; considered ideal but rarely natural; follows ideal Spee and Wilson curves; tripodized; P.K. Thomas's technique). Dr. Givan often builds cusp-marginal ridge on purpose, because multiple contacts help prevent supereruption. What cusp hits where: the fence post From the help sheet: unless told otherwise, assume Class I and an idealized cusp-fossa occlusion. Draw two rows of fence posts: canine, first premolar, second premolar, then the mesial and distal halves of the first and second molars, for each arch. In Class I each mandibular post sits a half step mesial to its maxillary partner (the mandibular canine slightly in front of the maxillary canine); Class II steps the mandible back one post; Class III brings it forward one tooth. "The only thing you really have to remember on fence posts is how to draw fence posts and what their canine relationships are." The fence post tells you which opposing cusp comes closest; it is not anatomical, and although the posts look like cusp-marginal ridge, exam questions are usually cusp-fossa. Then use your anatomy: Premolars, Class I and Class III: contacts in the mesial fossae of the maxillary premolars and the distal fossae of the mandibular premolars. Class II is the opposite. So in Class I the buccal cusp of #29 is in the mesial fossa of #4, and the lingual cusp of #5 is in the distal fossa of #28. Molars have an anterior and a posterior opposing contact. The maxillary first molar's posterior contact (from the DB cusp of #30) is highly variable, from the oblique ridge to the distal fossa. The mesiolingual cusp of #3 sits in the central fossa of #30. Anchor and step: to decide whether the MB cusp of #31 hits the mesial fossa of #2 or the distal fossa of #3, start at the first molar's posterior contact (DB of #30) and step back: it must be the mesial fossa of #2. Anterior relationships and anterior guidance Growth gives deep overbite, edge-to-edge, or an anterior open bite, properly an "anterior open occlusal relationship": no anterior contact in any occluding position of the posterior teeth ("a bite is a verb"). Vertical overlap (lay term overbite) of 3-5 mm is normal, 3 mm the most accepted; orthodontists often accept 1 mm to make room for lower brackets. Horizontal overlap is the lay "overjet." Together they set anterior guidance: the influence of the contacting anterior surfaces on mandibular movement, determined mostly by the lingual (palatal) morphology of the maxillary incisors. The joint, briefly The mandible has a body, angle, ramus, coronoid process and condyle. The temporomandibular joint is the articulation between the temporal bone and the condyle: a diarthrodial, bilateral ginglymus joint that both hinges and slides, with an avascular connective tissue disc between condyle and fossa. "I personally think, because I'm a dentist, that it's the most complicated, most difficult joint in the body." Eccentric movements and contacts Any movement away from the intercuspal (or seated) position is eccentric. Protrusive: the mandible moves forward and the condyle comes down the articular eminence, carrying the disc; posterior teeth that fail to separate contact on the distal inclines of the maxillary and mesial inclines of the mandibular teeth. Christensen's phenomenon is the space that opens between the posterior teeth in protrusion as the condyle drops down the eminence; Christensen is remembered for showing that a protrusive record captures the eminence angle. Retrusive: slightly back (posterior temporalis). In a lateral movement the working (laterotrusive) side is the side the mandible moves toward; its condyle mostly rotates. The non-working side (mediotrusive, "balancing," a denture term) is the other one; its condyle orbits: forward, down and medially along the eminence. Working-side contacts are on the side of the movement; non-working contacts are considered interferences. Help sheet method for interferences: draw the molars in MIP, then move the mandibular tooth in your mind's eye. For the right molars in a left working movement (right side non-working), a contact can occur between the facial incline of the maxillary palatal cusp and the lingual incline of the mandibular buccal cusp. In a right working movement, the lingual incline of the maxillary palatal cusp meets the buccal incline of the mandibular lingual cusp, and the facial incline of the mandibular buccal cusp meets the lingual incline of the maxillary buccal cusp (an interference if unwanted, group function if wanted). For protrusion draw a sagittal view; for crossbite move the mandibular molar to the buccal and reconsider. Cusp pathways: on a maxillary tooth you watch a mandibular cusp, so protrusive runs mesial, working runs buccal, non-working runs mesiopalatal. On a mandibular tooth you watch a maxillary cusp and everything reverses: protrusive runs distal, working lingual, non-working distobuccal. In a picture the MIP contact is at the base of the arrow: identify the movement first, eliminate choices, then identify the cusp. Guidance and the goals of ideal occlusion Canine guidance (canine-protected articulation): the vertical and horizontal overlap of the canines disengages the posterior teeth in excursions; canines have the buttressing bone and proprioception for it. Group function: several teeth share the working-side contacts (e.g. #7-6-5), useful when the canine has compromised periodontal support, is missing, or is an implant (no proprioception). Today group function means a few anterior teeth and perhaps the first premolar, not every tooth. Which has more influence on posterior separation, anterior or condylar guidance? The closer determinant has the greater impact: anterior guidance, when the patient has it. The list "you will see over and over": equal, simultaneous, stable centric contacts; occlusal force directed down the long axes; elimination of balancing contacts; canine disclusion or group function of the anterior (and occasionally posterior) teeth. Together that is mutually protected articulation: the posterior teeth protect the anterior teeth from excess force in MIP, and the anterior teeth disengage the posterior teeth in all excursions. Balanced occlusion is for dentures, not natural teeth. The determinants of posterior morphology Thielmann's formula: balanced occlusion = (condylar guidance × anterior guidance) / (cusp height × compensating curvature × plane of occlusion). Change one factor and the others must change. For natural teeth, the factors tell you how tall the posterior cusps can be: Condylar guidance Steeper Taller Anterior guidance More vertical overlap Taller Anterior guidance More horizontal overlap Shorter Plane of occlusion More parallel to the condylar guidance Shorter Curve of Spee More acute Shorter (the most posterior cusps) Bennett movement Greater, more superior, or greater immediate side shift Shorter Horizontal factors set the direction of ridges and grooves (the cusps must "escape" each other). A greater distance from the rotating condyle, a greater distance from the midsagittal plane, and a greater Bennett movement all increase the angle between a cusp's laterotrusive and mediotrusive paths; a greater intercondylar distance decreases it. That is why an articulator much smaller than the patient produces crowns you must adjust. Vertical dimension Vertical dimension of occlusion (VDO): the distance between two points with the teeth in contact; supports facial height. Vertical dimension at rest (VDR): the same measure at physiologic rest. Freeway space (interocclusal rest space) = VDR minus VDO, usually 2-6 mm; neither 2 nor 6 is "better." Posterior overclosure (old term posterior bite collapse): loss of occluding vertical dimension as posterior teeth are lost or drift, causing interferences and unhealthy loading; treatment starts by correcting the plane of occlusion. Mandibular movement and the envelope of motion Start from CR. Rotation (hinge movement) with the condyles seated opens the incisors about 20-25 mm. Beyond that the condyles must translate down and forward; rotation plus translation reaches about 40-60 mm. Border movements are the limits: the superior contact border is dictated by the teeth; the anterior and posterior opening borders by ligaments and joint anatomy. Posselt's envelope of motion (about 1958) combines the borders in the sagittal, horizontal and frontal planes. Sagittal view, tracing the lower incisor: from CR, pure rotation down to about 20-25 mm, then rotation plus translation to maximum opening (the posterior opening border). From maximum opening, closing with the jaw fully protruded traces the anterior opening border up to maximum protrusion. The superior contact border runs from the CO contact up and forward into MICP (if they differ), down the anterior guidance to edge-to-edge, flat forward past the incisal edges, then on to maximum protrusion. If CO equals MICP, the border runs straight from CR into the anterior guidance. Horizontal view (from above): left lateral, left lateral with protrusion, right lateral with protrusion, right lateral. Frontal view: left lateral superior, left lateral opening, right lateral opening, right lateral superior, with the postural position (PP) just below the top. Expect to identify these. We rarely function at a border, except the superior one. Function happens in a small teardrop below MICP, and most functional activities begin or end at MICP. The postural position is about 2-4 mm below MICP, held by a myotactic reflex against gravity so the teeth can be brought into function immediately. It is often wrongly called the clinical rest position, which is the position of least EMG activity, about 8 mm inferior and 3 mm anterior. Head posture changes the path of closure: in the "alert feeding position" the face is about 30° down, and contacts recorded supine can shift anteriorly when the patient sits up. Dr. Givan checks every restoration upright; about 20% of patients feel a difference. Mandibular lateral translation (Bennett movement, side shift and many other names) is the mediolateral shift of the mandible toward the working side. It may be immediate (a jump, measured in millimeters) or progressive (measured as an angle, the Bennett angle). It comes with joint laxity and its importance "is still somewhat controversial." Articulators 101 An articulator is a mechanical instrument representing the TMJs and jaws, to which casts are attached to simulate some or all mandibular movements. It is only really useful when it represents the patient; one much smaller than the patient moves differently, "convenient for a laboratory, but very inconvenient for the people who had to put it inside the patient's mouth." Parts of the Whip Mix 2240 (semi-adjustable): upper and lower members, anterior guide pin (not "incisal pin": "rude to the canines"), anterior guide table, mounting plates, condylar elements (with an articulating fossa) and the centric latch, which holds the instrument on its transverse horizontal hinge axis. "In occlusion, we're talking in the language of microns." You can feel a 25 µm hair between your teeth; "you have to be a micron dentist."
